0.summary: 15-year-old male presented to A&E on 07/01/26 at 08:45 with severe abdominal pain for 3 days. ED diagnosis was constipation. No known allergies, no current medications, and no past medical history documented. Plan was baseline observations and assessment of pain severity.

1.summary: 15-year-old male with abdominal pain. Focused abdominal assessment at 09:10 on 07/01/26 showed mild abdominal distension and lower abdominal tenderness, with no guarding or rebound tenderness. Advised NPO and plan to initiate IV fluids for mild dehydration pending further investigations.

2.summary: 15-year-old male with 3 days of abdominal pain. ED diagnosis: constipation. Triage noted mild dehydration. Focused abdominal exam showed mild abdominal distension and lower abdominal tenderness without guarding or rebound tenderness. Management included IV 0.9% sodium chloride 500 mL over 4 hours and keeping the patient NBM. Bloods and abdominal X-ray were pending for further management decisions.

3.summary: Abdominal X-ray on 2026-01-07 showed significant faecal loading. Findings were discussed with the patient and his mother. A single oral dose of bisacodyl 10 mg was given to initiate bowel movement, and IV 0.9% NaCl was continued for mild dehydration.

4.summary: 15-year-old male presented with 3-day history of lower abdominal pain and constipation, with reduced appetite and mild nausea but no vomiting or fever. Pain was constant, dull, worse with eating, and rated 7/10 initially. Exam showed mild abdominal distension, lower quadrant tenderness, mildly hypoactive bowel sounds, and mild dehydration with slightly dry mucous membranes and reduced skin turgor; no guarding, rebound, peritonism, or haemodynamic instability. Pain improved to 5/10 after IV fluids. Abdominal X-ray showed significant faecal loading with no obstruction or perforation. FBC, U&Es, CRP, and LFTs were normal. Impression was constipation with mild dehydration. Referred to paediatrics and admitted to paediatric ward for supportive management and observation. Plan: Movicol 1 sachet TID, encourage oral hydration, and monitor bowel movements; no surgery required.

5.summary: 3-day history of worsening constant dull lower abdominal pain, worse with eating, associated with constipation and reduced appetite. Pain was 6/10 on arrival, improving to 5/10 after IV 0.9% sodium chloride in the ED; a single 10 mg dose of bisacodyl was also given. No nausea, vomiting, melaena, haematochezia, urinary symptoms, or systemic symptoms reported. Examination showed a distended abdomen with mild bilateral lower quadrant tenderness, no guarding or rebound, tympanic abdomen, normal bowel sounds, and mild dehydration (dry mucous membranes, slightly reduced skin turgor). Vitals were stable. Abdominal X-ray showed significant faecal loading with no obstruction or perforation. Blood tests were normal (FBC, U&Es, CRP). Impression was constipation with associated abdominal pain and mild dehydration. Plan: oral macrogol 13.8 g sachets 1 sachet TID, encourage oral fluids, monitor bowel movements and symptoms, reassess after 24 hours, and consider further imaging or alternative laxatives if not improving.

6.summary: Seen on ward round for abdominal pain due to constipation. Abdominal X-ray showed significant faecal loading. Patient reported abdominal discomfort rated 5/10. Examination: alert and comfortable at rest; abdomen distended but soft with mild lower quadrant tenderness, normal bowel sounds, no guarding, rebound, peritonitis, masses, or organomegaly. Observations stable: HR 72, BP 112/68, RR 16, Temp 36.8, SpO2 99%. Plan: start oral macrogol 1 sachet BD, encourage at least 2 L/day oral fluids, monitor bowel movements, and reassess laxative dose if no improvement by next morning.

7.summary: Initial physiotherapy session on 07/01/26 at 15:30 focused on gentle mobilisation to aid bowel motility and relieve constipation. Patient completed light exercises including short-distance walking within the ward and seated leg lifts. Education was provided on the importance of regular movement to improve digestion and constipation symptoms. Session was tolerated well without adverse events. Plan: light walking every 2–3 hours as tolerated, with follow-up scheduled for 08/01/26 to assess progress.

8.summary: Nurse Jamie Leigh Alexander provided education to the patient and his mother on the importance of dietary fibre and hydration. Written materials on high-fibre foods and recommended fluid intake were given. No changes were made to the existing treatment plan.

9.summary: Seen on ward round for abdominal pain due to constipation. Patient had a partial bowel movement overnight and reports reduced abdominal pain and feeling more comfortable. Abdomen is less distended; on exam it is soft, mildly distended, with reduced lower quadrant tenderness and no guarding or rebound. Observations were stable: HR 82, BP 110/70, RR 16, Temp 36.8, SpO2 99%. No new investigations, imaging, or lab results. Plan: continue macrogol 1 sachet TDS, encourage oral hydration, assess for full bowel movement within 24 hours, and consider discharge if symptoms continue to improve.

10.summary: Physiotherapy review on 08/01/26 at 10:30 focused on promoting bowel motility and alleviating residual abdominal discomfort related to prior constipation symptoms. Patient was guided through gentle stretching exercises and light mobility activities for 20 minutes, with good tolerance and no adverse events. Advised to continue light walking post-discharge to support recovery and prevent symptom recurrence. No new medications prescribed.

11.summary: Dietitian reviewed the patient and advised a high-fibre diet, including whole grains, fresh fruits, and vegetables. No medication changes were made. Current plan of oral laxatives and hydration is to continue.

12.summary: Second physiotherapy session on 08/01/26 at 14:00 for residual abdominal discomfort and bowel motility. Patient completed 20 minutes of gentle stretching and light mobility exercises, participated actively, and reported reduced discomfort with movement compared with 07/01/26. No adverse events. Recommended continuation of light mobilization during hospital stay and gentle walking at home after discharge to support bowel motility.

13.summary: Presented with abdominal pain due to constipation, which resolved after a full bowel movement overnight. Patient reported no further abdominal pain and felt well. Observations were stable: HR 78, BP 112/74, RR 16, temp 36.6, SpO2 98% on air. Examination was unremarkable, with a soft, non-tender abdomen and no guarding or rebound. Plan was to stop oral macrogol, prescribe take-home lactulose 10 mL BD PRN for maintenance, and discharge today with advice on a high-fibre diet and oral hydration to prevent recurrence.

14.summary: Discharge communication was made with the patient’s GP, Dr. CianCian, by Nurse Jamie Leigh Alexander. The GP was informed of the patient’s discharge and hospital management, and follow-up arrangements were discussed to ensure ongoing management for constipation prevention. The patient and family were advised to contact the GP if constipation symptoms recur.

0.summary: 67-year-old man with history of hypertension and osteoarthritis, no regular medications and no allergies, presented to A&E at 07:30 after a minor fall with acute confusion. Initial vitals: BP 170/95, HR 88. Triage category 2 due to confusion and recent trauma. ED assessment diagnosed subdural hygroma; further assessment and investigations were planned, with review pending.

1.summary: 67M presented with acute confusion after a minor fall. On triage, GCS 12/15 with disorientation to time and place; BP 170/95 and pulse 88 bpm. Past medical history includes hypertension and osteoarthritis. No known drug allergies. Referred for urgent blood tests and CT head to rule out intracranial injury.

2.summary: 67-year-old man with acute confusion after a minor fall, triaged category 2. GCS 12/15 with disorientation to time and place. Past medical history includes hypertension and osteoarthritis. Initial blood draws were completed for investigation of possible intracranial injury, including FNC, electrolytes, and coagulation profile, and he was escorted to radiology for CT head scan to assess for possible subdural hygroma.

3.summary: 67-year-old male reviewed after CT head showing subdural hygroma; findings explained to patient. He remained comfortable but disoriented to time and place with GCS 12/15 (E4 V3 M5), following acute confusion after a minor fall. ABCDE assessment was otherwise stable: airway patent, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, BP 150/85, HR 82, CRT <2 seconds, warm peripheries, and no external injuries, rash, or bruising noted. Plan was handover to the medical team for admission to the Neurology Ward for further management.

4.summary: 67-year-old man with HTN and OA presented after a minor fall at home with acute confusion and disorientation to time and place. No loss of consciousness, headache, vomiting, visual changes, chest pain, palpitations, dizziness, seizures, or focal neurological symptoms. On arrival he was alert but mildly confused; initially GCS 12/15 in triage, improving to 14/15 on final assessment. Neurological exam showed pupils equal and reactive, cranial nerves intact, no focal deficit, normal tone/power/reflexes, no pronator drift, and no ataxia or postural instability. Vitals were stable aside from elevated BP (155/90; 170/95 in triage). CT head showed a subdural hygroma with no midline shift or acute haemorrhage; FBC, U&E, and coagulation profile were normal. Impression was subdural hygroma secondary to minor fall with acute confusion, without evidence of raised ICP or acute bleed. Accepted by neurology and transferred to Neuro Ward (Bed B09) for monitoring, with neuro obs 4-hourly, repeat CT head in 48 hours, mobilisation as tolerated, and escalation if confusion worsens or new neurological signs develop.

5.summary: Acute confusion after a minor fall at home the previous evening (~21:00) with no loss of consciousness. Neighbour found him confused the next morning, prompting 999 call. He reported a mild occipital headache since the fall but denied preceding dizziness, chest pain, weakness, nausea/vomiting, visual changes, incontinence, tongue biting, or recent illness. In ED, BP was 170/95 mmHg with initial GCS 12/15, improving to 13/15 during clerking. Exam showed him alert but mildly confused, GCS 13/15 (E4V4M5), with normal cranial nerves, tone, reflexes, plantar responses, coordination, and no focal neurological deficits or signs of head trauma; gait could not be assessed because he was unsteady. Observations were HR 82, BP 148/92, RR 16, temp 36.7, SpO2 97%. CT head showed a subdural hygroma with no midline shift or acute haemorrhage. FBC, U&E, and coagulation studies were normal. Impression was subdural hygroma secondary to minor fall, likely related to hypertension, with no acute complications. Plan: paracetamol 1 g QDS PO for headache, repeat CT head in 48 hours, close neurological monitoring, and MDT input if confusion persists.

6.summary: Acute confusion after a minor fall. CT head confirmed a subdural hygroma without acute complications. Mild hyponatremia present (serum sodium 132 mmol/L), felt to be contributing to confusion. On review, the patient reported mild confusion but was comfortable and cooperative. Observations were stable: HR 88, BP 140/85, RR 16, Temp 36.8, SpO2 98%. Exam showed the patient was alert but mildly confused, with intact cranial nerves II-XII, 5/5 motor strength in all limbs, intact sensation, normal reflexes and coordination, and no new neurological deficits; gait was not assessed. Plan: oral sodium chloride tablets 1 g TDS, repeat CT head in 48 hours, and physiotherapy referral for mobilization assessment.

7.summary: Physiotherapy assessment on 01/01/26 at 15:30 for mobility and balance after subdural hygroma and a recent minor fall. Mild gait instability was observed, with slight unsteadiness while walking a short distance and no significant risk of falls noted. Neurological status showed mild confusion and disorientation to time, but the patient was cooperative. Airway was patent, breathing unlaboured with RR within normal limits, cardiovascularly stable (BP 130/85 mmHg, HR 78 bpm), and no external injuries or skin breakdown were seen. Plan was to start daily physiotherapy focusing on balance and mobility exercises, with progress to be reviewed in subsequent sessions; MDT informed. No medications were initiated or adjusted.

8.summary: Next of kin Margaret Robinson phoned at 16:00 and was updated on the admission and current condition (SDH). No clinical questions were asked and no immediate actions were required.

9.summary: Occupational therapy assessment on 01/01/26 noted mild fine motor coordination impairment affecting ADLs, with difficulty fastening buttons and handling utensils. No significant gross motor deficits were identified. Plan is to initiate occupational therapy sessions to improve fine motor coordination and teach adaptive strategies for self-care tasks. No medication changes.

10.summary: Seen on ward round with acute confusion after a minor fall. Diagnoses/issues: subdural hygroma, clinically stable, with repeat CT head planned for 03/01/26; mild hyponatremia with serum sodium 132 mmol/L, felt to be contributing to confusion, with slow correction ongoing. Today he felt “a little better” but remained mildly confused. Exam: alert but disoriented to time, neurology observations stable with no focal deficits, gait mildly unsteady consistent with prior physiotherapy findings. Observations: HR 84, BP 140/85, RR 16, ताप 36.9, SpO2 98% on room air. Plan: continue slow sodium correction with NaCl 1 g TDS, daily physio and OT for balance and fine motor coordination, and reassess neurological status and sodium levels tomorrow.

11.summary:
Physiotherapy session on 2026-01-02 focused on balance and coordination. Patient completed a short assisted corridor walk using a walking frame, with slight improvement in stability compared with the 2026-01-01 session. Mild gait instability persists, but there was no evidence of acute fall risk.

ABCDE assessment: airway patent; breathing non-laboured with SpO2 97% on room air; circulation stable with BP 140/85 mmHg, HR 82 bpm, capillary refill <2 sec; neurological status unchanged with mild confusion persisting but patient cooperative and responsive to verbal cues; no new external injuries or skin issues identified.

Plan is to continue daily physiotherapy to improve balance, mobility, and gait instability, with close monitoring of progress.

12.summary: GP (Dr. Olonisakin) was updated regarding admission and management of the subdural hygroma. No change to the treatment plan. GP to coordinate follow-up after discharge.

13.summary: Speech and language assessment on 02/01/26 at 14:30 found swallowing function adequate, with an appropriate swallow reflex on water swallow test and no signs of aspiration. Communication assessment showed speech articulation and comprehension appropriate for age, with mild word-finding difficulty possibly related to residual confusion. No further speech or swallowing intervention was required at this stage; plan was to reassess word-finding difficulty if confusion persists.

14.summary: Ward round review for acute confusion after a minor fall with known subdural hygroma. The patient remained clinically stable with ongoing mild confusion and no new symptoms. Examination showed alert but mildly confused, no focal neurological deficit, no signs of raised intracranial pressure or meningism, and CVS/respiratory/abdominal examination was unremarkable. Observations were stable: HR 84, BP 140/88, RR 16, ताप 36.8, SpO2 97% on room air. Repeat CT head was scheduled later today to reassess the hygroma; blood tests were pending. Plan was to continue oral sodium chloride 1 g TDS, review CT results, and monitor for neurological changes or worsening confusion.

15.summary: Repeat CT head at 10:30 showed no progression of the subdural hygroma and no new findings. Reviewed by the specialty registrar; no change to management. Continue physiotherapy and occupational therapy.

16.summary: Occupational therapy initial assessment on 03/01/26 focused on discharge planning and home safety. The patient had mild difficulty with fine motor tasks, including handling small objects, and required moderate assistance for simulated tasks such as chair transfers. Raised toilet seat and bathroom grab rails were recommended for home safety. Follow-up session planned to reassess progress and provide further guidance on home safety modifications.

17.summary: Physical therapy session on 03/01/26 at 15:00 focused on balance and coordination exercises, including tandem walking and single-leg stance. Patient showed moderate improvement and completed exercises with minimal assistance. Exam findings: airway patent, no stridor or obstruction; breathing unlaboured, RR 14/min, SpO2 96% on air; BP 140/85 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, capillary refill <2 seconds; GCS 14/15; pupils equal and reactive to light; warm and dry with no acute pain or discomfort during exercises. Plan to progress to stair-climbing exercises in the next session to further assess and improve mobility and balance in preparation for discharge, with daily physiotherapy continued.

18.summary: Ward round for acute confusion. Known subdural hygroma; repeat CT head on 03/01/26 showed no progression, and neurological observations have been stable over the past 24 hours. Patient reports feeling more oriented with no new symptoms. Observed vitals: HR 82, BP 140/85, RR 16, temp 36.8, SpO2 98% on room air. On examination, patient was alert and cooperative with improved cognition compared with previous days, no focal neurological deficits, and mildly unstable gait. Plan: refer to social work for home assessment and discharge planning support, continue daily physiotherapy for balance/mobility and occupational therapy for ADLs/home safety adaptations, and reassess for possible discharge in coming days if stable.

19.summary:
Physiotherapy session on 04/01/26 focused on stair climbing to improve balance, coordination, and confidence. Patient ascended and descended one flight of five steps using a handrail, requiring minimal supervision and verbal cues for foot placement. Progress in mobility and balance was noted, with no adverse events. Mild residual confusion was present, consistent with prior assessments.  

ABCDE exam: airway patent; normal respiratory effort with no distress; BP 140/85, HR 82, no peripheral oedema; alert and oriented to person and place with mild residual confusion; no new signs of injury or discomfort.  

Plan: continue daily mobility exercises, increase stair-climbing difficulty as tolerated as part of discharge preparation, and continue next physiotherapy session for further mobility goals. No medication changes.

20.summary: Patient’s spouse, Margaret Robinson, visited the ward and was updated on the patient’s condition and planned discharge timeline. No clinical decisions required.

21.summary: Occupational therapy session on 04/01/26 focused on home safety education to reduce fall risk. Recommendations included removing loose rugs, ensuring adequate lighting throughout the home, and installing handrails on staircases and in bathrooms. The patient was instructed in use of a grabber tool to avoid overexertion and successfully practiced this under supervision. A referral was made for a home assessment to evaluate additional modifications or assistive devices.

22.summary: Acute confusion after a minor fall in the context of a subdural hygroma, with mild residual gait instability likely related to the hygroma and improved with physiotherapy. On review, the patient felt clearer in the head and was confident mobilising with supervision. Repeat CT head on 2026-01-03 showed no progression of the SDH. Observations were stable: HR 84, BP 138/78, RR 16, temp 36.8, SpO2 98% on room air. Examination showed the patient alert and oriented to person, place, and time, with mildly unsteady gait and no focal neurological deficit; cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal examinations were normal. Plan: start atorvastatin 40 mg once daily for 7 days for cardiovascular risk, continue physiotherapy for balance/mobility, continue occupational therapy for fine motor coordination and home safety assessment, and refer to social work for home assessment and discharge planning.

23.summary:
Final physiotherapy session for discharge readiness. Patient completed mobility assessment and exercises, including walking on flat surfaces and navigating small obstacles. Walked 15 m independently with steady gait, good balance, and coordination.  

Objective findings: airway patent; no respiratory distress; respiratory rate within normal limits; haemodynamically stable; capillary refill <2 s; GCS 15/15. Prior confusion has resolved; patient oriented to time, place, and person. No visible abnormalities or acute changes.  

Assessment/plan: cleared for independent mobility. Advised to continue light mobility exercises at home after discharge. No further physiotherapy sessions required. No new medications or treatment changes. Proceed with scheduled discharge planning per MDT recommendations.

24.summary: Discharge support was discussed with the patient with input from Nurse Hopkins. Recommendation: community support services after discharge.

25.summary: Functional assessment of ADLs performed on 05/01/26 at 14:00, including dressing, preparing a simple meal, and safe bathroom use. Patient demonstrated competence in gross motor tasks but had mild fine motor coordination impairment, especially with fastening buttons and handling utensils; no significant cognitive barriers were identified. Home safety education was provided, including fall-risk reduction measures (remove loose rugs, ensure adequate lighting, install handrails in staircases and bathrooms). Patient practiced using a grabber tool to reduce strain and overexertion. OT referral was made for a home assessment to evaluate need for additional modifications or assistive devices. Patient was deemed fit for discharge home with support services in place; no further OT sessions planned. No new medications prescribed.

26.summary: Presented with acute confusion after a minor fall. Known subdural hygroma with no progression on repeat CT head on 2026-01-03. Confusion was improving; patient felt better and was less confused. Blood tests earlier in the week showed no abnormalities. Vitals were stable. On examination, patient was alert and oriented with no focal neurological deficit, stable gait, independent mobility, and mild residual confusion. Discharge was confirmed for today. Plan: levetiracetam 500 mg BD for 7 days, discharge summary to patient and GP, neurology outpatient follow-up in 1 month, community support services for daily activities after discharge, and home safety adjustments including raised toilet seat and bathroom grab rails as advised by OT.

27.summary: Contacted GP Dr. Oluwaseun Olonisakin to update on the patient’s condition and confirm post-discharge neurology follow-up in 2 weeks.

28.summary: Patient education session provided by N. Hopkins on management of dizziness/confusion and prior falls at home. No change to treatment plan. Post-discharge safety advice given.

29.summary: Patient clinically stable with no residual confusion or neurological deficits. Discharge plans were reviewed and confirmed, with discharge planned for tomorrow. Follow-up in the neuro clinic has been arranged.

30.summary: Final physiotherapy session on 07/01/26 focused on assessing functional independence in mobility. ABCDE assessment was normal/stable: airway patent, breathing unlaboured with RR 16, CVS stable with HR 72 and BP 135/85 mmHg, neurologically intact with no confusion and GCS 15/15, and patient was independent in mobility with no distress or pain. Patient demonstrated full independence with walking 15 m, climbing 5 steps with handrail, and good balance during exercises including obstacle navigation. Education was provided on safe mobility techniques at home and strategies to reduce fall risk. Patient was deemed fit for discharge with no further physiotherapy needs and advised to continue light mobility exercises at home as tolerated.

31.summary: Discharge summary completed by Nurse Shaun Patrick Hopkins. No changes to medications or treatment plan. Follow-up in the neurology clinic is scheduled.

32.summary: GP Dr. Olonisakin notified regarding patient discharge. Hospital stay included management of a subdural hygroma. Follow-up appointment in neurology clinic arranged in 2 weeks.

0.summary: Admitted for elective left total hip replacement for end-stage osteoarthritis, with history of hypertension. On examination, patient was alert and not in acute distress; left hip deformity with tenderness, limited range of motion, inability to fully bear weight on the left side, but neurovascular exam intact and surgical-site skin intact without signs of infection. Observations: HR 75, BP 142/88, RR 16, Temp 36.8, SpO2 98%. Pre-op ECG showed normal sinus rhythm with no ischemic changes. Bloods showed mild anaemia (Hb 11.3 g/dL); other routine bloods were within normal limits. Plan was to proceed with scheduled L THR, maintain fasting pre-op, notify anaesthetic team, review post-op analgesia, monitor for post-op anaemia and consider iron replacement if Hb drops further, continue paracetamol 500 mg PRN and calcium with vitamin D supplements, and closely monitor blood pressure peri-operatively.

1.summary: Pre-op checklist completed on 02/01/26 at 08:15 for elective total left hip replacement for end-stage osteoarthritis. Identity confirmed by wristband and verbal confirmation; left hip confirmed as correct surgical site. Patient was fasting as instructed, all jewellery and removable prostheses removed, and no allergies reported. Current medications reviewed: paracetamol 500 mg PRN and calcium with vitamin D supplements. Hemoglobin had been optimised after a ferrous sulfate course; mild anaemia was previously noted but stable. Blood pressure was elevated but consistent with known hypertension with no acute concerns. Anaesthetic assessment found the patient suitable for spinal anaesthesia. Patient understood the procedure, risks, and benefits, with consent previously obtained. Patient was in stable condition and cleared to proceed to theatre for surgery at 09:00 as scheduled.

2.summary: Total left hip replacement performed via posterolateral approach under spinal anaesthesia for end-stage osteoarthritis of the left hip. Intraoperative findings showed severe degenerative changes with significant cartilage loss and no evidence of infection or abnormal surrounding tissue. The left femoral head was removed and sent for histological examination; a cemented prosthetic implant was placed in the left hip. The surgical site was closed in layers with subcuticular sutures and a sterile dressing applied. Estimated blood loss was approximately 150 mL, with no intraoperative complications. Post-operative plan included enoxaparin 40 mg SC once daily for thromboprophylaxis, regular paracetamol 1 g every 6 hours for pain control, early mobilisation with physiotherapy later today, and monitoring for infection, VTE, or other complications.

3.summary: 75-year-old woman after total left hip replacement under spinal anaesthesia. In PACU at 11:30 on 02/01/26, observations were stable: BP 130/85, HR 72, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air. She was alert, orientated, and communicating. No nausea/vomiting. No significant pain, only mild discomfort, treated with IV paracetamol 1 g. Surgical site was clean and dry with no bleeding. Cleared for transfer to Ward 3A. Early mobilisation with physiotherapy planned later the same day. Enoxaparin 40 mg SC once daily started for thromboprophylaxis.

4.summary: Postoperative ward review for severe left hip pain due to end-stage osteoarthritis. Patient reports mild surgical site pain (3/10), well controlled with paracetamol. Postoperative anaemia noted with Hb 104 g/L, felt likely secondary to surgical blood loss; other blood tests showed no abnormalities. Vitals stable: HR 72, BP 130/85, RR 16, Temp 36.9, SpO2 98% on room air. Exam: alert and oriented, dressing clean/dry with no bleeding or infection, mild tenderness at the surgical site. Plan: start ferrous sulfate 200 mg once daily, initiate physiotherapy for mobilisation later today, repeat Hb in 48 hours, and continue enoxaparin 40 mg SC once daily for thromboprophylaxis.

5.summary: 75F, POD0 after left total hip replacement. Initial physiotherapy session at 16:00 with Hazel Kayleigh Barton. Mobilised with a walker; short distance ambulation with support. Focused on safe weight bearing and adherence to hip precautions, including no greater than 90° flexion and no leg crossing. Patient cooperative. Plan for daily physiotherapy to progress mobility and build confidence with aids.

6.summary: Post-op update provided to the patient’s GP, Dr. Panashe Dhlamini, regarding recovery after total left hip replacement. Surgery outcome, current condition, and progress were discussed to ensure continuity of care. No immediate changes to the treatment plan were advised by the GP.

7.summary: Post-operative ward review after left hip end-stage osteoarthritis surgery. Pain is well controlled on paracetamol and the patient is mobilising short distances with a walker, with good adherence to hip precautions. Post-op anaemia noted with Hb 105 g/L, felt to be peri-operative; no acute intervention required and no other abnormal investigations. Vitals stable: HR 78, BP 134/86, RR 16, Temp 36.9, SpO2 98%. Exam showed alert, cooperative patient with wound clean/dry and no erythema or discharge, and no leg swelling. Plan: encourage oral hydration and iron-rich diet, continue daily physiotherapy, continue enoxaparin 40 mg SC once daily for thromboprophylaxis, and recheck Hb trend tomorrow.

8.summary: Physiotherapy session focused on stair navigation. The patient practiced ascending and descending two steps using a handrail and a walker. Proper posture and balance were emphasized. The patient showed improved confidence and strength compared with the previous session. No pain or safety issues were observed. Plan is to continue daily physiotherapy and progress to crutch use as tolerated. No new medications required.

9.summary: Next of kin Evelyn Chinwo was contacted by telephone for an update on Mrs. Chniwo’s post-operative progress. Discussed that she is in a stable condition with effective pain control and progress with physiotherapy. Anticipated discharge timeline was reviewed. No concerns were raised, and there were no changes to the treatment plan.

10.summary: Occupational therapy assessment on 03/01/26 at 14:30 following total left hip replacement on 02/01/26 focused on ADL ability post-surgery. The patient practiced safe bed mobility with minimal assistance, reaching for objects on a counter while maintaining hip precautions, and safe dressing using adaptive strategies with minimal assistance. Education was provided on hip precautions (avoid hip flexion beyond 90 degrees, internal rotation, and adduction), use of mobility aids for safety/fall-risk reduction, and strategies to maintain independence at home during recovery. Recommended home adaptations were a raised toilet seat and grab bars in the bathroom, with arrangements made for delivery prior to discharge. The patient understood the education, was cooperative, and continued OT input was planned with liaison to the discharge team to confirm home adaptations before discharge.

11.summary: Post-operative ward review for severe left hip OA. Mild stiffness with mobilisation; pain well controlled with paracetamol and patient adhering to physiotherapy. Post-op anaemia with Hb 105 g/L, felt likely due to peri-operative blood loss; no acute intervention required. Vitals stable: HR 72, BP 130/85, RR 16, Temp 36.8, SpO2 98%. Exam: alert, no distress, wound clean/dry with no erythema or swelling, no signs of DVT. Plan: progress to crutches for mobilisation, no medication changes, review tomorrow for further mobilisation progress.

12.summary: Physiotherapy session focused on gait training. Patient’s progress with walker-assisted mobilisation was assessed and he/she was deemed ready to advance to crutches. Education emphasized proper weight distribution and adherence to hip precautions. Patient transitioned from walker to crutches, demonstrated good balance and coordination, and had no issues following precautions. Patient was engaged and motivated. Plan is to continue using crutches for mobility, with further physiotherapy to build strength and confidence before discharge.

13.summary: Dietitian review of nutritional status. Advised a high-protein diet to support wound healing and muscle recovery, with inclusion of lean meat, fish, eggs, and legumes. Recommended nutritional supplements if appetite remains reduced.

14.summary: Seen by occupational therapy on 04/01/26 at 15:30 following total left hip replacement on 02/01/26. A hip kit (reacher, sock aid, long-handled shoehorn) was provided and demonstrated to support ADLs while maintaining hip precautions, including avoiding flexion beyond 90° and adduction. Patient practiced use of the tools and ADLs such as getting in/out of bed, reaching for objects, and dressing with minimal assistance, demonstrating understanding and competency. Advised to continue using the hip kit at home. Recommended minor home adaptations including a raised toilet seat and grab bars in the bathroom; delivery arrangements have been made. No adverse issues identified. No changes to medication or current therapy plan.

15.summary: Post-left total hip replacement for severe left hip osteoarthritis. Wound clean with no erythema, discharge, or swelling; no calf tenderness or swelling. Mobilising well with crutches. Minimal pain controlled with PRN paracetamol and confident with ADLs. Postoperative anaemia with Hb 10.8 g/dL; prescribed ferrous sulfate 200 mg OD and advised high-iron diet. Observations stable: HR 76, BP 132/86, RR 16, Temp 37.2, SpO2 98% on room air. Plan for discharge tomorrow with rivaroxaban 10 mg OD for 7 days and arranged follow-up physiotherapy.

16.summary: Final physiotherapy assessment at 09:30 focused on safe crutch use for ambulation, including gait practice, sit-to-stand from a chair, turning, and navigation of obstacles in a simulated home environment. Patient demonstrated good balance and coordination, no gait abnormalities, and adhered to post-op hip precautions, including avoiding hip flexion beyond 90 degrees and crossing the legs. Deemed safe for independent discharge with crutches. Plan to continue outpatient physiotherapy as scheduled. No medication changes required.

17.summary: Discharge planning meeting held with the patient and next of kin (daughter, Evelyn Chinwo). Consultant reviewed recovery progress and provided post-op care instructions. Follow-up physiotherapy plan and outpatient clinic appointments were explained. Emphasis was placed on hip precautions and continued use of crutches. Patient planned for discharge home on 06/01/26 with follow-up arrangements in place.

18.summary: Discharge education provided, including wound care, medication schedule, and mobility precautions. Patient was given discharge medications including Paracetamol 500 mg as needed for pain. Advised to adhere to discharge instructions and follow-up care plan. No new medications were prescribed.

19.summary: Pre-clerking for elective total left hip replacement for severe end-stage left hip osteoarthritis. History of gradual worsening left hip pain over 5 years, deep aching pain, constant and worse with prolonged standing/walking and weight-bearing, with limited mobility and stiffness; severity 8/10. Exam showed patient well, no distress; left hip pain on palpation and ROM with severe restriction in flexion and internal rotation, no redness or swelling. Lower limb pulses were palpable with no oedema or DVT signs; neuro exam showed 4/5 power at left hip flexion/extension due to pain, sensation intact. Observations stable aside from BP 145/85. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm with no ischaemic changes. Bloods notable for mild anaemia (Hb 11.3 g/dL); WCC, platelets, renal function, and LFTs were normal. Plan was to start ferrous sulfate 200 mg daily, contact GP for BP monitoring/optimisation, proceed with elective total left hip replacement, and have pre-op anaesthetic review on admission day.

20.summary: 75F seen pre-operatively for elective left total hip replacement for end-stage osteoarthritis. Past history includes hypertension, severe left hip osteoarthritis, and cataract surgery in 2018. She reported no recent shortness of breath or chest pain; mild fatigue was noted. Blood pressure was 145/85. Hemoglobin was 11.3, consistent with mild anaemia, and she was taking FeSO4. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm with no ischemic changes. Current medications were paracetamol PRN, calcium/vitamin D supplements, and FeSO4 200 mg once daily. No known drug allergies. She was assessed as suitable for spinal anaesthesia with no contraindications, and the procedure, risks, and benefits were explained; she consented. No medication changes were required.

21.summary: Pre-op consent obtained on 21/12/25 for total left hip replacement for end-stage osteoarthritis. Risks discussed included infection, blood clots, prosthetic joint complications (loosening, wear, dislocation), anaesthetic risks, and possible residual pain or leg length discrepancy. Benefits and recovery expectations were explained; patient asked about recovery timeline and post-op mobility, all questions were answered, and written informed consent was obtained. Current medications unchanged: paracetamol 500 mg PRN and calcium with vitamin D. Pre-op assessment showed mild anaemia (Hb 11.3 g/dL), being managed with ferrous sulfate 200 mg once daily, and BP 145/85 mmHg consistent with known hypertension. Cleared for spinal anaesthesia and for the pre-op checklist. Admission planned for 02/01/26 to Orthopaedic Elective Ward 3A, bed A07, with expected 4-day stay.

22.summary: Elective admission for total left hip replacement for end-stage left hip osteoarthritis. Pre-op assessment confirmed identity, procedure, and surgical site; no allergies reported. Past history includes hypertension and cataract surgery in 2018. Current medications reviewed: paracetamol 500 mg as needed for pain, calcium with vitamin D, and ferrous sulfate 200 mg once daily. Investigations showed mildly reduced Hb 11.3 g/dL consistent with mild anaemia; ECG showed normal sinus rhythm with no ischemic changes; BP 145/85 mmHg, mildly elevated. No contraindications identified and patient cleared for surgery on 02/01/26. Advised to continue ferrous sulfate until surgery for haemoglobin optimisation.

0.summary: Admission for planned total left hip replacement for end-stage osteoarthritis. On examination, the patient was well and in no acute distress, with no signs of infection. Cardiorespiratory exam was normal with normal heart sounds, no murmurs, and clear lung fields. Left hip had reduced range of motion consistent with OA, with intact skin and no swelling, bruising, or deformity. Observations were HR 76, BP 128/82, RR 16, Temp 36.7, SpO2 98%. Pre-op investigations were already completed; Hb was 10.8 g/dL indicating mild anaemia, and renal and LFTs were normal. Past medical history included HTN, hyperlipidemia, and mild osteopenia. Plan was to proceed with surgery, give IV cefuroxime 1.5 g within one hour before incision, keep the patient fasting per guidelines, stop ibuprofen 48 hours pre-op, and start omeprazole 20 mg daily for 2 weeks.

1.summary: Ward round review for end-stage osteoarthritis of the left hip, with planned total left hip replacement. Patient reports mild pre-existing left hip pain but no acute distress. Examination showed patient comfortable in bed, surgical site marked, left hip mildly tender with limited range of motion, and no swelling, erythema, or signs of infection. Mild anemia noted with Hb 11.2 g/dL; other results unremarkable. Observations: HR 84, BP 138/85, RR 16, Temp 36.8, SpO2 98%. Plan was to give TXA 1 g IV at time of surgery to minimize perioperative blood loss, proceed with surgery as planned, and make no changes to current medications.

2.summary: Elective left total hip replacement performed under general anaesthesia and spinal block for end-stage osteoarthritis of the left hip. Intraoperative findings showed severe cartilage erosion with subchondral bone exposure; no acute inflammation or infection in surrounding tissues. Damaged cartilage and subchondral bone from the left acetabulum and femoral head were removed, and a cemented total hip prosthesis with polyethylene acetabular component and metal femoral component was implanted. Estimated blood loss was 300 mL, with no complications noted. Post-operative care included enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily for 28 days, paracetamol 1 g QDS, tramadol 50 mg every 6 hours PRN, and IV cefuroxime 1.5 g for 24 hours. Plan was early mobilisation with physiotherapy, monitoring for infection/haematoma, and maintaining hydration and nutritional support.

3.summary: Post-op after elective total left hip replacement under GA on 03/01/26. In PACU, cardiovascular and respiratory status remained stable with BP/HR/RR within normal limits and O2 saturation 98% on room air; no respiratory distress. Estimated blood loss was 300 mL, managed without transfusion. Neurologically drowsy but rousable, following simple commands, with no focal deficits. Pain 4/10 on NRS improved after IV morphine 2 mg. Post-op analgesia started with paracetamol 1 g QDS, ibuprofen 400 mg TDS, and tramadol 50 mg PO 6-hourly PRN for breakthrough pain. No nausea/vomiting or evidence of bleeding. Enoxaparin 40 mg SC commenced for VTE prophylaxis and IV cefuroxime 1.5 g prescribed for 24 hours post-op. Transferred to T&O Ward A for ongoing post-op monitoring and routine care.

4.summary: Post-operative day 1 following total left hip replacement for end-stage left hip osteoarthritis. Patient comfortable with no new complaints; pain well controlled on oral analgesics. Observations stable: HR 78, BP 132/84, RR 16, temp 36.8, SpO2 98% on room air. Examination showed intact surgical wound dressing with no erythema, swelling, or discharge; no calf tenderness or swelling; no systemic signs of infection. No investigations performed or pending. Plan: continue enoxaparin 40 mg SC once daily for thromboprophylaxis, regular paracetamol 1 g QDS, tramadol 50 mg Q6H PRN for breakthrough pain, cefuroxime 1.5 g IV for 24 hours post-operatively, encourage mobilisation with physiotherapy tomorrow, and review in 24 hours.

5.summary: Initial postoperative physiotherapy session on 03/01/26 at 14:00 on T&O Ward A following elective total left hip replacement. Early mobility exercises were initiated to aid recovery and prevent complications, including sitting at the edge of the bed, ankle pumps, and gentle leg lifts. A walker was provided and the patient took first assisted steps within the room, bearing partial weight on the left leg with minimal discomfort. Compliance was good and no adverse events occurred. Plan was to continue supervised physiotherapy twice daily with goal of assisted walking using a walker by 04/01/26. No medication changes.

6.summary: Post-op occupational therapy assessment after total left hip replacement to evaluate need for home adaptations for safe discharge and recovery. During simulated home activity assessment, the patient had difficulty with low seating and limited ability to reach overhead cabinets. Activities trialed included getting in and out of a mock car, use of a raised toilet seat, and simulated use of a long-handled reacher. Recommendations were for a raised toilet seat, grab rails in the bathroom, and a long-handled reacher. The patient engaged well and understood the recommendations. Referral made to the community OT team to ensure adaptations are installed prior to discharge.

7.summary: Post-operative review after total left hip replacement for end-stage left hip osteoarthritis. Pain is well controlled and the patient is mobilising with a walker and assistance. Surgical site is clean and dry with no erythema or discharge; mild swelling is present but within expected limits, with no tenderness around the operative site and no signs of DVT. Vitals stable (HR 78, BP 126/78, RR 16, Temp 37.1, SpO2 98%). Hb 10.8 g/dL with mild post-operative anaemia/drop. Plan: ferrous sulfate 200 mg once daily for 4 weeks, encourage increased oral fluid intake, and continue supervised physiotherapy progressing to weight-bearing exercises with walker today.

8.summary: Physiotherapy session on 04/01/26 at 10:00 focused on progressing to partial weight-bearing exercises using a walking frame, with balance training, gait training, and confidence-building in mobilisation. The patient completed short supervised walks with the frame and showed improved weight distribution and control during ambulation. No excessive pain or discomfort was reported, and compliance/motivation were good. Plan was to continue weight-bearing exercises twice daily and progress to stair practice at the next session on 05/01/26. Earlier the same day, ferrous sulfate 200 mg once daily for four weeks was prescribed for mild anaemia (Hb 10.8 g/dL). No adverse events were noted.

9.summary: OT session on 04/01/26 focused on safe transfer techniques. The patient practiced bed-to-chair, sit-to-stand, and toilet transfers, including use of a raised toilet seat and a chair with armrests to mimic home adaptations. She was supervised throughout, received feedback for safety and proper mechanics, remained compliant, and no issues were noted. Plan is to continue practicing transfer techniques in daily therapy. No medication changes were required.

10.summary: Post-operative review following total left hip replacement for end-stage left hip OA. Pain is satisfactorily controlled on paracetamol 500 mg twice daily; patient has no new concerns and is mobilising short distances with a walker and managing transfers independently. Surgical wound is clean and dry with no erythema, swelling, or discharge; no fever or other systemic signs of complication. No calf tenderness or swelling. Observations stable: HR 78, BP 132/80, RR 16, temp 36.8, SpO2 98% on room air. Hb 10.8 g/dL, consistent with mild post-operative anaemia; no other abnormalities. Plan: stop ibuprofen 400 mg, start dalteparin 5000 units SC for thromboprophylaxis until discharge, continue physiotherapy, and review tomorrow for discharge planning.

11.summary: Post-THR stair training session on 05/01/26 with Therapist Patrick Malcolm Shah. Focus was safe stair navigation at home using a handrail and walker, with emphasis on correct weight distribution over the left hip and step mechanics. Patient demonstrated satisfactory progress, able to ascend and descend a simulated staircase with appropriate use of walker and handrail, maintaining good posture and following instructions. No pain exacerbation or discomfort reported; no adjustment to analgesia needed. Medication update: paracetamol 500 mg twice daily continued, ibuprofen 400 mg discontinued, and dalteparin 5000 units SC continued for thromboprophylaxis until discharge. Plan for final OT review in the afternoon and continued gradual mobility progression toward independent stair navigation before discharge.

12.summary: Final OT review on 05/01/26 at 15:00: patient demonstrated independent and safe performance of ADLs at home using adaptive equipment previously provided, including a raised toilet seat and long-handled reacher. Successfully completed dressing independently, performed bed-to-chair transfers safely without assistance, and prepared simple meals without difficulty. No issues identified; patient was compliant and confident. Cleared for independent ADLs at home with no further OT sessions, referrals, or home adaptation changes needed prior to discharge.

13.summary: Post-operative review following total left hip replacement for end-stage left hip osteoarthritis. Patient feels well with pain well-controlled on current analgesia. Surgical wound is clean, dry, and healing well with no erythema, swelling, discharge, or signs of infection/complications. Demonstrated safe ambulation with a walker. Vitals stable (HR 78, BP 132/84, RR 16, Temp 36.8, SpO2 98%). Chest clear, abdomen soft and non-tender, and no signs of DVT in the lower limbs. No investigations performed today. Plan: discharge today with TTOs including apixaban 2.5 mg BD for 2 weeks, continue home exercise programme, and GP follow-up in 6 weeks for wound review and outpatient physiotherapy referral.

14.summary: Final mobility training session focused on safe crutch use and independent stair navigation. Patient practiced ascending and descending stairs under supervision with attention to proper weight distribution on the operated hip, and crutch technique was reviewed and demonstrated for safe ambulation. Home exercise program for hip strength and flexibility was reviewed with demonstration. Patient was actively engaged, understood the mobility techniques and exercises, reported no acute pain, and mobilized with minimal discomfort. Patient was able to navigate stairs and ambulate independently with crutches, meeting discharge criteria for mobility. Advised to continue the prescribed home exercise program; no further therapy sessions required.

15.summary:
Pre-operative assessment for severe left hip pain due to end-stage osteoarthritis, with gradual worsening over 4 years causing constant deep aching pain, stiffness, reduced range of motion, difficulty walking, and pain up to 8/10. Planned procedure: total left hip replacement, scheduled for 02/01/26.

Past history: hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and mild osteopenia. Current analgesia: paracetamol 500 mg twice daily and ibuprofen 400 mg as needed. No known drug allergies.

Exam: comfortable at rest with slightly antalgic gait; left hip tender with reduced ROM, especially internal and external rotation, and mild left thigh muscle wasting. No effusion or erythema. Neuro: left lower limb power 4/5 due to pain, otherwise normal reflexes and sensation. CVS, respiratory, and abdominal exams were unremarkable.

Observations: HR 78, BP 145/90, RR 16, temp 36.8, SpO2 98%.

Investigations: ECG showed normal sinus rhythm without ischaemia or arrhythmia; urinalysis normal. Routine pre-op bloods showed mild anaemia with Hb 10.8 g/dL; renal and liver function tests were normal.

Plan: start ferrous sulfate 200 mg once daily for anaemia, GP review of antihypertensive medications to optimize BP before surgery, continue current analgesics as needed, and encourage gentle exercises/mobility within pain limits.

16.summary: Pre-operative anaesthetic assessment for elective total left hip replacement for end-stage osteoarthritis. Past history of hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and mild osteopenia; no previous anaesthetic complications and no known drug allergies. Medications: paracetamol 50 mg twice daily and ibuprofen 400 mg as needed. BP was 148/92 mmHg. Pre-op review showed mild anaemia with Hb 10.8 g/dL; ECG and urinalysis were normal. Anaesthetic plan was general anaesthesia combined with spinal block, with no contraindications identified. Recommendations: start omeprazole 20 mg once daily for 2 weeks, continue antihypertensive management and GP follow-up for BP optimisation prior to surgery, and continue ferrous sulfate 200 mg once daily for mild anaemia. Patient was counselled on the anaesthetic plan and risks and consented to proceed.

17.summary: Consent discussion for elective total left hip replacement for end-stage osteoarthritis. Procedure, purpose (pain relief and improved mobility), surgical steps, and anaesthetic plan (general anaesthesia plus spinal block per earlier assessment by Dr. Hannah Freda Dixon) were explained. Relevant history includes hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and mild osteopenia. Pre-op assessment found no contraindications to anaesthesia. Recent labs showed mild anaemia with Hb 10.8 g/dL, and ferrous sulfate 200 mg once daily had been started. Blood pressure was moderately elevated at 148/92 mmHg; review of antihypertensive medication was recommended. Omeprazole 20 mg daily was started for 2 weeks to reduce GI side effects from ibuprofen. Risks discussed included infection, DVT, prosthesis loosening/wear, possible future revision surgery, and standard anaesthetic risks; benefits discussed included pain relief, improved joint function, and better quality of life. Patient’s questions about post-op pain control and recovery were addressed, she confirmed understanding and willingness to proceed, and consent was signed. Plan was to proceed to the pre-operative checklist and continue BP monitoring plus ferrous sulfate and omeprazole.

18.summary: Pre-op checklist completed for planned total left hip replacement for end-stage osteoarthritis, with admission/surgery scheduled for 02/01/26. Current medications reviewed: paracetamol 500 mg twice daily and ibuprofen 400 mg as needed; advised to stop ibuprofen 48 hours before surgery to reduce bleeding risk. No known drug allergies. Fasting instructions reviewed. Signed consent form confirmed, obtained by Dr Elizabeth Kathryn Singh on 20/12/25. Planned anaesthetic approach is GA combined with a spinal block. No new medications prescribed.

0.summary: 3-year-old male presented to A&E with poor feeding and mild lethargy reported by parent. Initial nursing assessment at 08:45 on 06/01/26 noted no immediate respiratory distress and no evidence of severe dehydration. Triage category was 3, with referral for triage to assess vital signs and urgency of further evaluation. Allergies: pollen and macrolides. No current medications and no past medical history documented.

1.summary: 3-year-old male presented to A&E with poor feeding and fever. Triage at 09:15 on 06/01/26 was Category 3. Observations: ताप 38.3°C, HR 120 bpm, SpO2 98% on room air. Known allergies: pollen and macrolides. ED assessment was viral illness. Paracetamol suspension 120 mg/5 mL, 5 mL dose was given for fever, with plan to monitor response.

2.summary: 3-year-old male presented with poor feeding. Initial nursing assessment showed mild lethargy without respiratory distress or severe dehydration. Triage observations: temperature 38.3°C, heart rate 120 bpm, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Allergies: pollen and macrolides. Given a 10 mL/kg normal saline fluid bolus via oral syringe for mild dehydration, which was well tolerated with no adverse effects. Plan to start oral rehydration solution (ORS) in small, frequent doses.

3.summary:
3-year-old boy presented with 24 hours of reduced oral intake, refusing fluids, fewer wet nappies, and mild lethargy. Parents reported mild fever; no vomiting, diarrhoea, respiratory distress, choking, or aspiration.

On examination he was alert and interactive, mildly lethargic but consolable, with dry mucous membranes and mild dehydration (CRT about 2 seconds). No respiratory distress, no abdominal tenderness or distension, no neck stiffness or photophobia, and fontanelle normal. Observations: HR 120 bpm, RR 22/min, ताप 38.3°C, SpO2 98% on room air.

No investigations were performed in ED. Impression was viral illness with associated mild dehydration and reduced oral intake. He received paracetamol suspension 120 mg/5 mL, 5 mL, and an oral normal saline bolus 10 mL/kg. He was accepted to Paediatric Assessment Unit for observation and supportive care, with plan for IV 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% dextrose, ORS in small frequent doses, paracetamol as required, and no antibiotics.

4.summary: Presented with 48 hours of poor feeding, reduced wet nappies over the last 24 hours, and mild lethargy. No vomiting, diarrhoea, rash, cough, shortness of breath, palpitations, cyanosis, or seizures. Exam showed the child was alert but quiet, mildly dehydrated with dry mucous membranes and capillary refill about 2 seconds, mild nasal congestion, clear chest, soft non-tender abdomen, normal tone and movement, GCS 15. Observations: HR 120, BP 95/60, RR 24, temp 38.3, SpO2 98%. Impression was viral illness with mild dehydration due to poor intake/reduced urine output. Plan: IV maintenance fluids (0.9% NaCl + 5% dextrose) at 75% maintenance, paracetamol suspension 5 mL QDS PRN for fever, monitor fluid status/intake-output, and reassess in 6 hours. U&Es, FBC, and CRP were pending.

5.summary: Seen on ward round for poor feeding in the setting of viral URTI. Child remained febrile and reluctant to feed, with no vomiting or diarrhoea; oral fluid intake had improved slightly after IV fluids. Exam showed alert but mildly lethargic child with dry lips, slightly delayed capillary refill (~3 sec), mild tachycardia, nasal congestion with mucosal swelling/minimal discharge, soft non-tender abdomen, and no respiratory distress. Observations: HR 115, BP 90/50, RR 34, temp 37.9, SpO2 98%. VBG showed mild metabolic acidosis with pH 7.33 and bicarbonate 17 mmol/L; no other blood abnormalities. Assessment included viral URTI, mild dehydration, and mild metabolic acidosis. Plan was IV maintenance fluids (0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose at 75% maintenance), paracetamol suspension 15 mg/kg every 6 hours PRN, nasal saline drops PRN, encourage oral hydration, and reassess hydration status and intake the next day.

6.summary:
3-year-old male reviewed on 06/01/26 at 15:00 for poor feeding and nutritional needs. Parents reported reduced oral intake and fewer wet nappies over the prior 24 hours. He was admitted with mild dehydration and poor feeding due to suspected viral illness and was receiving IV fluids. Initial bloods showed mild metabolic acidosis with pH 7.33 and HCO3 17 mmol/L.

Advice given: small, frequent oral feeds with easily digestible foods; oral rehydration solution in small regular sips; encourage preferred fluids; nasal saline drops for congestion affecting feeding; parents educated on signs of dehydration.

Plan: continue IV fluids as prescribed, administer ORS as discussed, use 0.9% saline nasal drops 2 drops per nostril as needed, monitor hydration status and oral intake, and review if poor feeding persists or dehydration worsens.

7.summary: Brief parental education provided to Jack’s parents on recognizing early signs of dehydration, including reduced wet nappies and lethargy. Demonstrated oral rehydration with small, frequent sips of ORS and advised continuing small, frequent oral fluids. Parents were instructed to monitor for improvement or worsening.

8.summary: Seen on ward round for poor feeding in the setting of a viral illness with mild dehydration. Parents reported improved oral intake overnight, with fluids and mashed food tolerated well; no fever overnight and hydration status improved. Mild nasal congestion persisted. Observations were stable: HR 102, BP 91/58, RR 22, temp 36.9, SpO2 98% on room air. On examination, the child was alert and interactive, with no respiratory distress, moist mucous membranes, soft non-tender abdomen, and no peripheral pitting oedema. No investigations were performed. Plan was to reduce IV fluids to 50% maintenance to encourage oral intake, give PRN paracetamol 120 mg q6h for fever/discomfort, continue nasal saline drops 0.9% 2 drops each nostril PRN, and monitor hydration status with review tomorrow.

9.summary: Persistent nasal congestion with intermittent nasal discharge affecting feeding, with poor oral intake, reduced wet nappies, mild dehydration on admission, and mild fever (38.3°C) that improved during the ward course. ENT assessment showed moderate nasal mucosal inflammation on anterior rhinoscopy, consistent with viral URTI, with no purulent discharge, anatomical abnormalities, or respiratory distress. VBG showed pH 7.33 and HCO3 17 mmol/L. Management was supportive: continue saline nasal drops, add saline spray for nasal irrigation, advise steam inhalation twice daily, and use paracetamol PRN for fever. Parents were educated on nasal irrigation and steam inhalation, and hydration/feeding status was to be monitored. Allergies: pollen and macrolides.

10.summary: Advice provided to Jack Gray’s parents on home management of a viral illness, emphasizing small, frequent oral feeds to maintain hydration. They were instructed to continue nasal saline drops and current hydration strategies, and to seek further medical attention if symptoms worsen or if there are signs of deterioration such as reduced wet nappies or increased lethargy. No new medications or interventions were started.

11.summary: Ward round review for poor feeding due to viral URTI. Parents reported Jack was more active and alert with improved oral intake. He remained afebrile (37.2°C) with persistent mild nasal congestion causing slight discomfort. Observations: HR 110, BP 90/55, RR 22, SpO2 98%. Examination showed he was alert, interactive, hydrated, with no respiratory distress and no other abnormalities noted. No investigations were done. Plan was discharge tomorrow, prepare discharge summary, prescribe paracetamol 120 mg/5 ml suspension PRN for home use, continue saline nasal drops, start nasal irrigation with saline spray, advise steam inhalation twice daily, and provide hydration and feeding advice at discharge.

12.summary: Final nursing observation and discharge checklist were completed at 08:00 by Nurse Hilary Toni Gilbert. Vital signs were clinically stable, and hydration status was without concerns. Parents understood the discharge instructions and had no questions. Patient was deemed ready for discharge; no new medications were prescribed. Parents were advised to continue saline nasal drops as per ENT recommendations.

13.summary: Reviewed for poor feeding due to viral URTI. Symptoms improved today with better eating and drinking, no difficulty reported. Mild nasal congestion persists. Child was clinically well and afebrile, alert and playful, with no signs of dehydration and clear chest. Observations: HR 100, BP 90/60, RR 22, Temp 36.8, SpO2 98%. Plan was discharge today with oral fluids/small meals, saline nasal drops PRN, nasal irrigation with saline spray, and steam inhalation twice daily. No new medications prescribed.

14.summary: Discharge summary finalized and provided to parents with verbal explanation. Parents were advised to contact GP Dr. Liu Tao if symptoms worsen or if there are concerns about hydration or feeding.

0.summary: 49-year-old male presented to A&E at 21:15 on 02/01/26 with acute confusion after a minor fall. On assessment, GCS was 14/15 with mild disorientation. Past medical history includes hypertension and mild osteoarthritis. No allergies reported. He was triaged as Category 2 (Emergency) and initial triage with neurological observation was planned.

1.summary: Brief neuro assessment at 21:30 showed persistent disorientation with GCS 14/15, unchanged from initial ED arrival. No other focal neurological deficits noted. Presenting complaint was acute confusion after a minor fall. CT head scan was escalated to rule out intracranial injury.

2.summary: 49-year-old male with acute confusion after a minor fall. Neurological observations at 22:00 by Nurse Dawn Yvonne Gibbs showed GCS 14/15 with mild decrease and documented disorientation. Decision made to expedite CT head scan to confirm the cause of acute confusion and assess for intracranial pathology.

3.summary: Routine neurological observations completed on 2026-01-02 at 23:15. GCS 14/15 with mild disorientation and slightly delayed bilateral pupillary light response. No acute deterioration observed. Planned handover to the medical team for admission and further neurological monitoring.

4.summary:
49-year-old man with history of hypertension and mild osteoarthritis presented with acute confusion after an unwitnessed minor fall earlier the same day. He denied loss of consciousness, headache, nausea, limb weakness, vertigo, prior confusion, seizure history, visual change, chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath, cough, abdominal pain, dysuria, or haematuria.

On examination he was alert but disoriented to time and place, GCS 14/15 (E4 V4 M6), with slightly delayed pupillary reaction to light but otherwise normal pupils and no focal neurological deficits. No signs of head trauma, papilledema, or neck stiffness; cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal exams were unremarkable. Observations were stable.

CT head showed a subdural hygroma with no midline shift and no acute bleed. FBC, U&Es, LFTs, and CRP were all within normal limits.

Assessment was subdural hygroma causing acute confusion, likely secondary to the minor fall. He was accepted to the Neuro Ward for further care and observation. Plan included IV paracetamol 1 g QID for pain, close neuro observations, no antibiotics, and no surgical intervention required.

5.summary:
Presented with acute confusion after tripping over a loose carpet edge at home on 02/01/26, with no loss of consciousness but feeling dazed afterward. Over the following hours he developed progressive confusion and poor recall of recent events, without headache, visual change, nausea/vomiting, limb weakness, chest pain, palpitations, or shortness of breath. He also reported mild right knee pain.

Past history includes hypertension and mild osteoarthritis; no regular medications and no allergies. On examination he was alert but mildly confused, GCS 14/15 (disoriented to time), dehydrated with dry mucous membranes, and had an unsteady gait requiring assistance. Cranial nerves, power, sensation, reflexes, coordination, cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, and meningeal examinations were otherwise unremarkable.

Observations were stable: HR 88, BP 142/86, RR 16, Temp 36.8, SpO2 98% on room air. CT head showed a subdural hygroma with no midline shift. Blood tests were normal apart from mild hyponatremia (Na 132 mmol/L); FBC, CRP, LFTs, coagulation profile, and glucose were normal.

Assessment was acute confusion secondary to subdural hygroma and mild hyponatremia, likely worsened by dehydration. Plan was IV 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L over 8 hours, IV paracetamol 1 g QID, neurological observations with 4-hourly GCS, repeat U&E in 24 hours, encourage oral hydration after IV fluids, monitor for focal neurological deficits, and liaise with neurology.

6.summary: Acute confusion after a minor fall with mild gait instability. CT head confirmed a subdural hygroma without midline shift. Patient reported confusion but denied headache or significant pain. Exam: alert but mildly disoriented, GCS 14/15 (E4 V4 M6), cranial nerves intact, mild gait instability, otherwise normal airway/breathing/circulation and no oedema or skin changes. Observations stable (HR 84, BP 132/78, RR 16, Temp 36.8, SpO2 98% on air). Mild hyponatraemia (Na 132 mmol/L) and slight dehydration noted; IV 0.9% sodium chloride started for correction. Plan included ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily for 5 days prophylactically, physio referral for mobility/balance assessment, and repeat U&Es in 48 hours while monitoring hydration.

7.summary: Physiotherapy assessment on 03/01/2026 for post-fall mobility and balance. Guided exercises included sit-to-stand transitions, tandem walking, and balance drills. Mild unsteadiness was noted during tandem walking, but tasks were completed with minimal assistance. No acute neurological signs were observed. Plan is for daily physiotherapy sessions focusing on balance and gait training to improve stability and reduce fall risk.

8.summary: Occupational therapy assessment at 11:30 noted mild difficulty with fine motor tasks, including fastening buttons. The patient managed ADLs with verbal prompts. A button hook tool was recommended, and follow-up OT was scheduled to monitor progress.

9.summary: Acute confusion after a minor fall, with CT-confirmed subdural hygroma and no midline shift. Neurological status remained stable with no focal deficits. Today the patient reported mild fatigue only, denying headache, nausea, or vision changes. Exam: alert, mildly fatigued but engaging; cranial nerves II-XII grossly intact; no focal neurological deficits; limb power 5/5 bilaterally with normal tone and reflexes; no obvious gait instability noted. Vitals were stable (HR 82, BP 128/78, RR 16, T 36.7, SpO2 98% on air). Plan was to encourage oral fluids for mild hyponatremia, repeat U&Es in 24 hours, continue prophylactic ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily for day 2 of 5, daily physiotherapy for balance and gait training, OT follow-up for fine motor tasks, and provide a button hook for dressing assistance.

10.summary: Second physiotherapy session post-admission focused on gait stability. Patient performed slow walking with a Zimmer frame, emphasizing weight distribution and step coordination. Required moderate assistance but showed slight improvement compared with the first session. No acute neurological symptoms were observed. Plan is to continue physiotherapy twice daily to improve balance and mobility. No new medications.

11.summary: Provided education on fall prevention, including home safety, safe use of assistive devices, and identifying environmental hazards. No changes to treatment or medications. Therapy sessions will continue as planned.

12.summary: Seen on ward round for acute confusion after a minor fall. Diagnosed with subdural hygroma and mild hyponatremia; sodium was 132 mmol/L and remained slightly low, with other blood tests within normal limits. Today the patient reported feeling well with no confusion or new complaints. Observations were stable (HR 78, BP 128/82, RR 16, temp 36.8, SpO2 98% on air). Examination showed the patient was alert, oriented, and cooperative, with no focal neurological deficits; gait remained mildly unsteady without acute worsening, and cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Plan was to start oral sodium chloride 1 g tablets TID, encourage increased oral fluid intake, and repeat blood sodium in 24 hours.

13.summary: Physical therapy session at 10:30 focused on lower limb strengthening. Exercises included seated leg raises and resistance band work, with posture guidance provided to prevent strain. Patient tolerated exercises well, with no acute distress or neurologic symptoms. Goal is to improve mobility in preparation for independent mobility. Plan is to progress to dynamic balance exercises at the next session to further enhance mobility.

14.summary: Social worker met with the patient to discuss discharge planning and assessed home safety and potential support needs. Plan is for social worker to coordinate with OT for a home safety visit prior to discharge.

15.summary: OT session on 2026-01-04 focused on adaptations for ADLs. Airway was patent; respirations 18/min with SpO₂ 98% on room air. BP was 142/90 mmHg and HR 116 bpm. Earlier CT head showed no abnormalities. No rash or external trauma was noted.

Observations: BP 145/92 mmHg, HR 118 bpm, temperature 38.9°C, RR 18, SpO₂ 98% on room air.

CT head was normal. Lumbar puncture showed CSF WCC 450 cells/µL predominantly neutrophils, glucose 1.5 mmol/L, and protein 1.2 g/L; cultures and blood cultures were pending. Impression: bacterial meningitis.

Admitted to the Neurology Ward under Dr Afua Asare. IV ceftriaxone 2 g twice daily and vancomycin were initiated, with IV fluids, antiemetics as needed, and monitoring for seizures or neurological deterioration.

Plan: discharge tomorrow with co-amoxiclav 500/125 mg three times daily for 7 days, co-codamol 30/500 mg for analgesia, and dalteparin 5,000 units subcutaneously once daily for 7 days post-discharge. Stop ibuprofen. Arrange outpatient follow-up in 2 weeks and provide a home physiotherapy plan.

20.summary:
Final physiotherapy review on 09/01/2026: Patient demonstrated correct independent technique for prescribed postoperative right shoulder exercises, including pendulum swings, passive arm raises, and isometric exercises. Reported mild discomfort without significant pain. Advice provided on analgesia (paracetamol or co-codamol 30/500 mg), pacing, positioning, and continuing omeprazole. Sling use and precautions were reviewed.

Discharged with a home exercise programme to be performed three times daily. Advised to avoid heavy lifting with the operated arm for six weeks. Prescribed a 7-day course of dalteparin injections for thromboprophylaxis. Follow-up outpatient physiotherapy scheduled for 16/01/2026. Patient understood the instructions and felt confident continuing rehabilitation independently.

21.summary: Discharge paperwork completed. Patient received verbal and written postoperative instructions, including wound care and continuation of home physiotherapy exercises. Advised to attend outpatient follow-up clinic in 6 weeks.

22.summary:
Preoperative assessment for planned total right shoulder replacement for end-stage osteoarthritis. The patient has several years of constant right shoulder pain (up to 8/10) with stiffness, restricted range of motion, impaired sleep, and difficulty with overhead activity and lifting. Examination showed right shoulder deformity, tenderness, severe restriction of abduction and external rotation, and crepitus; right upper-limb sensation and motor function were intact.

Past history includes hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, osteoarthritis, and cataract surgery (2018). Current medications are paracetamol 1 g QDS, ibuprofen 400 mg TDS with food, and omeprazole 20 mg OD. Allergy: nuts. Observations were stable (BP 138/84, HR 76, SpO₂ 97%). ECG showed minor age-related changes without acute abnormalities. Blood tests showed mild anaemia (Hb 11.2 g/dL), with normal U&E and coagulation profile.

Ferrous sulfate 200 mg BD was started, with advice to increase dietary iron intake. Continue antihypertensive and lipid-lowering therapy. Proceed with surgery on 05/01/26; repeat preoperative blood tests on admission to confirm haemoglobin optimisation.

23.summary:
76-year-old man assessed preoperatively on 23/12/25 for elective total right shoulder replacement on 05/01/26. Medical history includes well-controlled hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, osteoarthritis, prior cataract surgery, and chronic mild anaemia (Hb 11.2 g/dL). ECG showed minor age-related changes without acute abnormalities. Allergy: nuts. Medications: paracetamol, ibuprofen, omeprazole; continue ferrous sulfate 200 mg twice daily.

Examination was unremarkable: patent airway, normal respiratory status, regular HR 74 bpm, BP 136/82, no murmurs or oedema, alert and neurologically intact, no infection concerns, BMI 26.

Risks of general anaesthesia, including age- and comorbidity-related cardiovascular and respiratory complications, were discussed and consent obtained. Fasting and medication instructions provided, with dietary advice for anaemia. Plan is to proceed with general anaesthesia and commence enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously once daily on admission for thromboprophylaxis.

24.summary: On 23/12/2025, informed consent was obtained for upcoming total right shoulder replacement for end-stage osteoarthritis. The procedure, expected benefits (pain relief and improved mobility), and risks (infection, bleeding, and nerve damage) were discussed, including recovery timeline and physiotherapy. The patient demonstrated understanding and had no further concerns. He was advised to stop ibuprofen from 30/12/2025 to reduce perioperative bleeding risk.

25.summary:
76-year-old man scheduled for elective total right shoulder replacement for end-stage osteoarthritis on 05/01/26. Hb was 11.2 g/dL, consistent with mild anaemia likely due to chronic disease; ferrous sulfate 200 mg twice daily was started. Anaesthetic assessment found no significant contraindications, with general anaesthesia planned. Enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously once daily is prescribed from admission for thromboprophylaxis.

Allergy: nuts. Regular medications include paracetamol, ibuprofen and omeprazole; ibuprofen is to stop 7 days preoperatively from 30/12/25. Written consent obtained after discussion of risks and benefits. Fasting and medication instructions reinforced. Relevant history includes hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, osteoarthritis and cataract surgery. Plan is to proceed with surgery as scheduled.

0.summary:
2-year-old male admitted electively to Paediatric Orthopaedics for Ponseti casting of the left clubfoot, scheduled for 07/01/26. He was alert, cooperative, and well appearing. 1.summary: Patient with congenital left talipes equinovarus remained stable overnight without complications and was well, comfortable, alert, and interactive on review. Left foot/leg and cast were satisfactory, with intact skin and no redness, swelling, infection, irritation, pressure sores, or defects. Remained NBM, with planned Ponseti casting under general anaesthesia at 08:00.

2.summary: Under general anaesthesia, Ponseti casting was performed for congenital left clubfoot. Foot alignment was corrected as expected, with no abnormal findings, incision, tissue removal, implants, blood loss, or complications. Postoperatively, oral paracetamol 120 mg every 6 hours as needed for pain and ibuprofen 100 mg every 8 hours as needed for inflammation were advised. The cast is to remain in place with monitoring for skin irritation or compromised circulation. Follow-up with paediatric orthopaedics is planned in 1 week to assess the cast and progress.

3.summary: Post-Ponseti casting for left clubfoot under uneventful general anesthesia. No complications. Deemed stable for transfer to Ward 3B.

4.summary: Left congenital talipes equinovarus (clubfoot) reviewed. Patient comfortable and alert with stable observations (HR 110, BP 92/60, RR 22, temperature 36.7°C, SpO₂ 99%).
